summary: A quieter day: the Bank of Canada explains why it is keeping its 2% inflation goal to 2031, and the Alberta and Ontario premiers pitch an all-Canadian oil pipeline.
body: Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem told the Economic Club of Canada in Toronto on Tuesday why the Bank and the federal government have renewed the 2% inflation target for another five years, from 2027 to 2031.[^1] He said shocks such as trade conflicts, wars and extreme weather are likely to become more common and can push prices up while slowing the economy at the same time, so the Bank must judge whether a price jump will fade or spread. It will keep aiming at total inflation, near 2%, and has added a public dashboard of other price measures.[^1] The Bank's October forecast has inflation around 3% through much of 2027, back near 2% by mid-2028. Interest rates on loans and mortgages follow from these choices.[^1]

On Monday Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Ontario Premier Doug Ford promoted the proposed Northern Shield pipeline, which would carry about 500,000 barrels of oil a day roughly 3,300 km from Hardisty, Alta., to Sarnia, Ont., without crossing the US.[^2] Ontario is leading a $17-million feasibility study, but no company has signed on, financing is unclear and Manitoba, which the line would cross, has not agreed.[^2] Both premiers admitted trade barriers between provinces remain: Smith said Alberta stores sell over 1,000 Ontario alcohol products while the LCBO stocks 53 from Alberta.[^2]

Last week Ottawa and Ontario each pledged about $464 million toward Ford Motor Company of Canada's nearly $5-billion plan to retool its Oakville plant to build Super Duty pickup trucks. The governments say it protects more than 2,000 jobs.[^3]
differences: Supporters say the pipeline would cut reliance on the US; Manitoba wants Indigenous partnership first, and commentators in The Hub say industry is wary after past cancellations.[^2]

reads.summary: What the two premiers said about the proposed pipeline and about the trade rules that still slow goods and workers moving between provinces.
